en: In the *Aṣṭāvakragītā*, Janaka said: "How did you obtain such knowledge? And how will liberation come to pass?"
And how was dispassion attained? Tell me this, O Lord.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
"O dear one, if you desire liberation, abandon sense-objects like poison;
cultivate forgiveness, uprightness, compassion, contentment, and truth as if they were nectar."
Know that for the sake of liberation, you are not earth, nor water, nor fire, nor air, nor sky, nor even the self; rather, know the Self to be the witness of these, whose nature is consciousness.
If, having separated yourself from the body, you remain resting in consciousness,
then this very moment you will become happy, peaceful, and liberated from bondage.
You are not a caste such as a brahmin, nor are you one belonging to a stage of life (āśrama), nor are you within the range of the senses.
You are unattached, formless, and the witness of the universe; be happy!
Dharma and adharma, pleasure and pain, and mental states do not belong to you, O All-pervading Lord; you are neither the agent nor the enjoyer, for you are eternally liberated.
You shall be the sole seer of all; you are, for all time, as if already liberated. For this alone is your bondage: that you perceive the seer as something other [than yourself].
Bitten by the great black serpent of the conceit "I am the doer," become happy by drinking the nectar of confidence that "I am not the doer."
With the fire of the certainty that "I am the one, pure awakening," burn away the thicket of ignorance; free from sorrow, be happy.
That consciousness in which this entire universe appears as imagined, like a snake in a rope, and which is supreme bliss and ultimate joy—that you are; conduct yourself in happiness. 1.10
For one who possesses the conceit of being liberated is indeed bound, as is one who possesses the conceit of being bound.
What can be said here regarding reality? Whatever the mind is, that shall be the destination.

The Self is the witness, all-pervading, complete, one, liberated, consciousness, and inactive; it is unattached, desireless, and peaceful, yet appears as if possessed of worldly existence due to delusion. (Avg 1.12)
Contemplate the Self as the immutable, non-dual consciousness;
having abandoned the delusion that "I am a mere appearance," [abandon] both external and internal existence.
"My son, you have long been bound by the fetter of identification with the body;
cut that asunder with the sword of knowledge, realizing 'I am consciousness,' and become happy. (Avg 1.14)
You are unattached, actionless, self-luminous, and stainless;
yet this very [state] is your bondage, for you remain engaged in meditative absorption.
This entire universe is pervaded by you and woven upon you in reality;
you are of the nature of purity and awakening— do not fall into a base state of mind.
Free from dependence, changeless, full, with a cool disposition,
possessing unfathomable intelligence and unshakable, become one whose latent impression is pure consciousness alone.
Know that which has form to be false, but that which is formless to be immovable;
through this instruction on reality, there is no further occurrence of rebirth.
Just as that [reflection] is within and all around the form situated upon a mirror,
even so is the Supreme Lord within and all around this body.
Just as the one all-pervading space exists both outside and inside a jar,
so too does the eternal and uninterrupted Brahman exist within the entire multitude of beings.
Janaka said:
"Aha! I am the stainless, peaceful awakening, beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
For all this time, I have been merely mocked by delusion."
Just as I alone illuminate this body, so do I illuminate the world;
therefore, the entire world belongs to me, or else it does not belong to me at all.
Alas! Having now abandoned the entire universe along with my own body, I perceive the Supreme Self through some skillful means alone. (Avg 2.3)
Just as waves, foam, and bubbles are not distinct from water, so too this universe, having emerged from the Self, is not distinct from the Self. (Avg 2.4)
Just as a cloth, when analyzed, is found to be nothing more than its threads,
so too this entire universe, when analyzed, is found to be nothing more than the self.
Just as sugar is fashioned from the juice of sugarcane and is therefore permeated by it,
so too the universe is fashioned within me and is pervaded by me without interval.

The world appears due to ignorance of the Self; it does not appear through knowledge of the Self. Just as a snake appears due to ignorance of a rope, but does not appear at all once that [rope] is known. (Avg 2.7)
Luminosity is my own nature; I am not distinct from it.
When the universe shines forth, I am indeed that very light.
Aha! Out of ignorance, the manifold world imagined by me appears within me, just as silver in mother-of-pearl, a snake in a rope, or water in the rays of the sun.
The universe has emerged from me alone and will return to dissolution within me, just as a jar [dissolves] into clay, a wave into water, and a bracelet into gold. (Avg 2.10)
"Aha! Obeisance to me, for whom there is no destruction, even as the world—from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—is perishing. (Avg 2.11)
Aho! I am he; salutation to me! Though I am alone and possess a body, I go nowhere and come from nowhere, remaining pervading the entire universe.
"Aha! Homage to me! There is no one here as skillful as I, by whom the universe has been sustained for a long time without even touching it with his body. (Avg 2.13)
"Aha! Praise be to me, who possesses nothing at all;
or rather, praise be to me, whose everything consists of that which falls within the range of speech and mind."
Knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower—this triad does not exist in reality. That in which this [triad] appears due to ignorance, I am that stainless one. (Avg 2.15)
Alas, the root of duality is suffering; there is no other remedy for it.
All this that is perceived is false; I alone am the stainless essence of consciousness.
"I am pure consciousness alone; through ignorance, a limiting adjunct has been imagined by me.
For one who constantly reflects in this way, my state is established in the non-conceptual. (Avg 2.17)
For me there is neither bondage nor liberation; delusion has been stilled and is without support.
Aha! The entire universe resides within me, yet in reality it does not reside within me.
It is certain that this entire universe, together with the body, is nothing at all;
and since the self is pure consciousness alone, where is there now any room for conceptual construction? (Avg 2.19)
The body, heaven and hell, bondage and liberation, and likewise fear—all this is merely a mental construction; what concern is it to me, whose nature is consciousness?
"Aha! Even amidst a multitude of people, for me who perceives no duality, the world has become like a forest; where, then, shall I find delight? (Avg 2.21)
I am not the body, nor is the body mine; I am not the living soul, for I am indeed consciousness.
This very longing for life was my bondage. (Avg 2.22)
Alas! While I am the infinite great ocean, the wind of the mind has suddenly arisen, causing the various waves of the world to surge forth. (Avg 2.23)
When the wind of the mind subsides within me, the infinite great ocean, the merchant-soul’s fragile ship of the world perishes through misfortune. (Avg 2.24)
Within me, the infinite great ocean, the waves of living beings arise, subside, sport, and enter by their very nature—a marvel indeed. (Avg 2.25)
Aṣṭāvakra said: Having realized in truth the one, indestructible Self,
how could there be any delight in the acquisition of wealth for you, a wise man who knows the Self?
Alas, from ignorance of the self, there is delight in the sphere of delusion regarding sense objects;
just as, through ignorance of mother-of-pearl, there is greed for it when it is mistaken for silver. (Avg 3.2)
Having realized that "I am He," in whom this entire universe vibrates like waves in the ocean— why do you run about like one who is miserable?
Even having heard that the self is pure consciousness and exceedingly beautiful, one who is intensely attached to the sexual organ falls into impurity. (Avg 3.4)
For the sage who perceives himself in all beings and all beings in himself, it is a marvel that the sense of "mine-ness" still persists.
Established in supreme non-duality and intent even upon liberation,
it is a marvel that he has become a slave to desire and rendered powerless by the practice of amorous play.
Perceiving that the enemy of knowledge has arisen and being extremely weak, one should,
with great wonder, desire death while awaiting the end of time.
For one who is dispassionate toward this world and the next, who discriminates between the eternal and the non-eternal,
and who desires liberation, it is a marvel that fear arises from liberation itself.
But the steadfast person, even while being fed upon or oppressed at all times,
seeing only the self, neither rejoices nor becomes angry.
He views his own active body as if it were the body of another;
how could one of such great magnanimity be disturbed by praise or blame? (Avg 3.10)
Seeing this entire universe as mere illusion, the wise-minded person, free from curiosity, how could they tremble even when death is imminent? (Avg 3.11)
For that great-souled one whose mind is free from longing even in the face of despair, and who is satisfied by the knowledge of the Self—whom can he be compared to? (Avg 3.12)

Knowing by its very nature that this visible world is nothing at all, what does that person of steadfast intellect see when it comes to "this is to be grasped" or "this is to be abandoned"? (Avg 3.13)
For one who has internally abandoned all passions, who is free from the pairs of opposites, and who is without expectations,
enjoyment that comes by chance leads neither to suffering nor to satisfaction.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
Alas! There can be no equality between one who knows the Self, who is steadfast and sports with the play of worldly enjoyments, and the foolish commoners of saṃsāra.
Alas, the yogi who abides in that state which all the deities, beginning with Śakra, seek in their wretchedness, does not experience joy. (Avg 4.2)
For one who knows that, no contact with merit or demerit arises within;
for there is no union of space with smoke, even though it appears to be so.
Who would be able to restrain that great-souled one by whom this entire world is known as the Self alone, and who proceeds according to his own will? (Avg 4.4)
Within the fourfold assembly of living beings, from the Brahma-world down to a blade of grass,
only the wise person possesses the capacity to remain free from both desire and aversion.
Someone who knows the self as non-dual and as the Lord of the world—whatever that person knows, they bring it about; for them, there is no fear anywhere.
Aṣṭāvakra said: You have no attachment to anything; why do you wish to abandon that which is pure?
Dissolving this very aggregate, go to dissolution in this very manner.
The universe arises from the Lord like a bubble from the ocean;
knowing the Self to be thus one, go to dissolution in this very way. (Avg 5.2)
Even though it is directly perceived, the universe does not exist within you, who are stainless, because it lacks substantial reality;
it is as manifestly unreal as a snake in a rope. In this very way, undergo dissolution.
Equal in suffering and happiness, full [in contentment], the same toward hope and despair,
equal in life and death— being thus, go indeed to dissolution.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
"I am infinite like space; the manifested world is like a jar.
Such is his knowledge; for him there is neither renunciation nor grasping, nor dissolution.
"I am like the great ocean, and that conceptual proliferation is like its waves"—such is his knowledge; thus for him there is neither rejection nor grasping, neither dissolution nor emergence.
"I am that which resembles mother-of-pearl, while the conceptualization of the universe is like silver"—such is his knowledge; for him, there is neither rejection nor grasping, nor dissolution.
"I am in all beings, and all beings are in me"—such is his knowledge; for him, there is neither renunciation nor grasping, neither dissolution nor emergence.
Janaka said:
In me, who am like the infinite great ocean, the boat of the universe wanders here and there driven by the wind of my own mind; yet I have no intolerance for this.
In me, the infinite great ocean, let the world-waves arise by their own nature and let them subside; there is neither increase nor decrease for me.
In me, the infinite great ocean, that which is called the universe is merely a conceptual construction;
I abide as this very state—utterly peaceful and formless.
There is no self in phenomena, nor are phenomena there in that infinite, stainless state;
thus, unattached, desireless, and peaceful, I exist as this very [reality].
Aha! I am indeed nothing but consciousness, and this world is like a magician’s illusion.
Therefore, how and where could there be for me any conceptualization of what is to be rejected or accepted?
Aṣṭāvakra said:
Bondage occurs when the mind desires something, grieves, releases something, grasps something, becomes arrogant, or becomes angry. (Avg 8.1)
Then there is liberation when the mind neither desires nor grieves,
neither releases nor grasps, and neither rejoices nor becomes angry.
Then there is bondage when the mind is attached to any views;
then there is liberation when the mind is unattached to all views. (Avg 8.3)
"When there is no 'I', then there is liberation; when there is an 'I', then there is bondage. Thinking thus, do not grasp at anything with indifference, nor let go of it. (Avg 8.4)
Aṣṭāvakra said:
When and for whom are the dualities of the done and the undone ever stilled?
Knowing this, become one who is intent on renunciation here, free from vows, and disenchanted.

O dear one, for a certain fortunate person, through observing the activities of the world, the desire for life, the craving for enjoyment, and the thirst for knowledge have all come to rest. (Avg 9.2)
Having determined that "all this is indeed impermanent, afflicted by the threefold suffering, essence-less, censurable, and to be abandoned," one attains peace. (Avg 9.3)
What is that time, or what is that age, in which dualities do not exist for men? Having disregarded those [dualities], how might one who acts according to whatever arises attain perfection? (Avg 9.4)
Having seen the various opinions of the great seers, as well as those of the virtuous and the yogis, what man would not become disillusioned and find peace?
Having brought about the thorough knowledge of the nature of consciousness, why is he not a teacher—
he who, through the application of detachment and equanimity, delivers one from cyclic existence?
Behold the modifications of the elements and the mere elements as they truly are;
at that very moment, you will be liberated from bondage and established in your own true nature.
"Samsara is nothing but latent impressions (vāsanā); therefore, abandon them all.
Their abandonment comes from the abandonment of latent impressions; let your state remain as it is today."—Avg 9.8.
Aṣṭāvakra said: Having abandoned desire, which is an enemy, and wealth, which is fraught with misfortune,
as well as dharma, which is the cause of both, practice total disregard for them in all circumstances.
Behold the riches of friends, fields, wealth, houses, wives, heirs, and so forth, for three or five days, as being like a dream or a magician’s net. (Avg 10.2)
Know that wherever there is craving, there indeed is saṃsāra;
relying on mature dispassion, become one who is free from craving and thus happy. (Avg 10.3)
Bondage consists solely of craving;
its destruction is called liberation. Through mere attachment to existence, there is a repeated satisfaction in acquisition. (Avg 10.4)
You alone are the conscious, pure one, while the universe is insentient and likewise unreal;
even ignorance is nothing at all—nevertheless, why do you still desire to know?
Kingdoms, sons, wives, bodies, and pleasures—
though you were deeply attached to them, they have perished for you birth after birth.
Enough with wealth, with desire, and even with well-performed deeds;
within this wilderness of saṃsāra, my mind has found no rest from these.
How many births have not been spent in performing actions that bring suffering and exhaustion through body, mind, and speech? Let such deeds cease even now.
Aṣṭāvakra said: One who has reached the certainty that change— whether existence or non-existence— arises from one's own nature,
being free from transformation and having transcended affliction, attains peace through very great ease.

One who is certain that the Lord alone is the creator of all and that there is no other here, with all expectations dissolved within, remains peaceful and does not cling to anything whatsoever. (Avg 11.2)

One who is certain that both misfortunes and successes occur in their proper time through destiny alone remains eternally content with healthy faculties; such a person neither longs for anything nor grieves. (Avg 11.3)

One who is certain that pleasure and pain, as well as birth and death, arise solely from destiny, who perceives nothing to be achieved and remains free from exertion, is not defiled even while acting. (Avg 11.4)
"Suffering arises from anxiety and not otherwise"—one who is certain of this, being free from it, is happy and at peace, with all longing dissolved in every respect. (Avg 11.5)
"I am not the body, nor is the body mine; I am pure consciousness"—one who is certain of this has attained liberation as it were, and no longer remembers what was done or left undone.

Having the firm conviction that "I alone am everything from Brahmā down to a blade of grass," he is free from conceptual construction, pure, peaceful, and liberated from both what has been attained and what has not been attained.
Having reached the certainty that this universe of manifold wonders is nothing at all,
one who is free from latent tendencies and consists of mere manifestation becomes tranquil, as if nothing exists.
Janaka said:
"At first, I was unable to endure bodily activities; then, I was unable to endure the expansion of speech; then, I was unable to endure thought. Therefore, I have remained exactly thus."
Due to the absence of pleasure in sound and the like, and because the self is invisible,
my heart remains thus fixed solely in a state of distraction and one-pointedness.
When distracted by the lack of concentration and so forth, my worldly activity was for the sake of concentration;
having observed this rule in this way, I have remained established in it exactly thus.
O Brahmin, because of the absence of both the rejectable and the acceptable, and likewise due to the non-existence of joy and dejection, I have now established myself in this very state.
Having observed the stages of life and non-stages, meditation, the mind's rejection of its own transformations, and conceptual construction, I have established myself in this very way.
Just as the performance of ritual action arises from ignorance, so too does its cessation;
having correctly understood this reality, I have established myself in this very way.
Even when contemplating the inconceivable, it takes on the form of thought;
therefore, having abandoned that contemplation, I remain established in this very state.
In the same way, he by whom that which was to be done has been done becomes one who has accomplished his purpose;
in the same way, he whose nature is such becomes one who has accomplished his purpose.
Janaka said:
"The state of self-abidance arising from possessing nothing is difficult to attain even while wearing only a loincloth.
Therefore, having abandoned this taking and giving, I shall remain as I am, according to my ease."

If there is weariness of the body anywhere, or if the tongue is weary somewhere, or if the mind is weary somewhere— having abandoned that, one who remains steadfast in human endeavor (puruṣārtha) finds happiness. (Avadānaśataka 13.2)
Reflecting on the reality that nothing at all has been truly accomplished,
when the time comes to do whatever must be done, perform it and remain at ease.
For the yogi established in the body, there is no longer any attachment to action or inaction;
because of the absence of both union and disjunction, I abide in happiness as it is.
"Neither by standing, walking, nor lying down do gain or loss accrue to me;
therefore, whether standing, walking, or sleeping, I shall remain as I am, at ease. (Avigraha 13.5)
There is no loss for me in sleeping, nor is there success for one who exerts effort; having abandoned both ruin and exultation, I shall remain as I am, in happiness. (Avigīta 13.6)
Having observed the frequent necessity of pleasure and its opposites in all things,
I shall abandon both the auspicious and the inauspicious and remain as I please.
Janaka said:
He whose mind is by nature empty, yet who through negligence cultivates the notion of existence,
is like one who has been awakened from sleep, for his memory has indeed faded away.
Where are my riches? Where are my friends? Where are the thieves of the sensory realms?
Where are the scriptures and where is my realization, now that all longing has dissolved from me? (Avg 14.2)
Since the Supreme Self, the Lord, has been realized as the witness-person,
and since there is no longer any hope regarding bondage or liberation, I have no further concern for my own release.
For one who is empty of internal conceptualization and wanders at will in the external world,
those various states are known just as they are, like those of a person under delusion.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
One who possesses the intelligence of a being of pure essence (sattva) achieves his purpose through instruction, however it may be given;
yet another, though desiring to know even for the duration of his life, remains utterly bewildered therein.
Liberation is the distaste for sense objects; bondage is the flavor of sense objects.
Knowledge consists of nothing more than this; do as you wish.
This awakening to reality makes eloquent, wise, and highly energetic people mute, dull, and indolent; therefore, it is rejected by those who desire worldly enjoyment. (Avg 15.3)
You are not the body, nor is the body yours; you are neither the enjoyer nor the doer.
You are the nature of consciousness, the eternal witness, independent; move about in happiness.
Attachment and aversion are qualities of the mind; they never belong to you.
You are non-conceptual, the very essence of awakening, and changeless; proceed in happiness.
Having realized yourself in all beings and all beings in yourself,
free from the sense of "I" and free from the sense of "mine," may you be happy.
That in which this entire universe vibrates like waves in the ocean—that you alone are; there is no doubt. O embodiment of consciousness, be free from the fever of doubt.
Have faith, dear one, have faith; do not fall into delusion in this matter.
The Blessed One is the very nature of knowledge; you are the Self, beyond primordial nature.
The body, enveloped by the qualities (guṇas), remains, comes, and goes;
the self neither goes nor comes—why do you grieve for it?
Let the body remain until the end of the eon, or let it depart this very day;
where is there growth or decay for you, whose nature is pure consciousness alone?
In you, the infinite great ocean, the waves of the universe arise and subside by their very nature; yet for you, there is neither increase nor diminution.
O dear one, you are of the nature of pure consciousness; this world is not distinct from you.
Therefore, for whom, how, and where could there be the conceptualization of what is to be rejected or accepted?
In you, the one, immutable, peaceful, and stainless sky of consciousness,
whence is birth, whence is action, and whence even the sense of "I"?
Whatever you perceive there, it is you alone who appears therein;
for how could bracelets, armlets, and anklets appear as something separate from the gold? (Avg 15.14)
Abandon the distinction between "this is I" and "this is not I";
having resolved that "all is the Self," be happy, free from conceptual construction.
The universe exists solely through your own ignorance; in ultimate reality, you alone are one.
There is no transmigrating being other than you, nor is there anyone who is not a transmigrating being. (Avg 15.16)
One who is certain that this entire universe is mere delusion and nothing at all—
being free from latent tendencies and consisting of mere manifestation— becomes tranquil, as if nothing exists.
In the ocean of existence, you have been, are, and will be only one;
you have neither bondage nor liberation. Having accomplished all that was to be done, live in happiness.
O you who consist of consciousness, do not agitate the mind with conceptualization and discursive thought;
be at peace and abide happily in your own self, whose form is bliss.
Abandon meditation altogether; do not hold anything whatsoever in your heart.
You are the Self and are already liberated; what will you achieve by further reflection? (Avg 15.20)
Aṣṭāvakra said:
"Tell me, my dear father, or listen to me; you have studied various scriptures many times over, yet even so, there is no peace for you except through the forgetting of everything."
Whether you practice for enjoyment, for karma, or for meditative concentration, O wise one,
nevertheless your mind will find it exceedingly pleasing when all desires have been cast out.
Through exertion, everyone suffers; no one knows this [truth].
Only by this very instruction does the fortunate one attain peace.
Happiness belongs only to that person who is foremost among the lazy and who is weary even of the opening and closing of his eyes; it does not belong to anyone else.
When the mind is freed from the dualities of "this has been done" and "this has not been done," it then becomes indifferent toward virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
One who is dispassionate is a hater of sense objects; one who is passionate is greedy for sense objects. But one who is devoid of both grasping and liberation is neither dispassionate nor passionate.
The sprout of the tree of saṃsāra— namely, the state of regarding things as either to be avoided or to be adopted—
indeed persists as long as there exists a state of longing that is the locus for the absence of discernment.
For passion arises toward worldly involvement, and indeed aversion toward liberation;
thus the wise man, free from the pairs of opposites, remains established just like a child.
One who is still subject to passion desires to abandon cyclic existence out of a wish to escape suffering;
for one free from passion is without suffering and does not even weary of that [cyclic existence].
He who possesses pride even regarding liberation and likewise a sense of "mine" regarding the body, is neither a man of knowledge nor a yogi; he is merely a partaker of suffering.
Even if Hara, Hari, or even the Lotus-born were your teacher,
nevertheless, there would be no peace for you except through the forgetting of everything.
Aṣṭāvakra said: He has obtained the fruit of knowledge as well as the fruit of the practice of yoga—
he who is ever content, whose senses are self-controlled, and who delights in solitude.
Alas, the knower of reality never suffers in this world, because by him alone is this entire circle of the universe filled. (Avg 17.2)
These sense objects never delight one who finds joy within himself,
just as neem sprouts do not please an elephant that delights in sallakī shoots.
But he who, when enjoyments have been experienced, is not stained by them,
and who has no longing for those not yet experienced— such a person is difficult to find in this world.
In this cycle of existence, one is seen who desires enjoyment, and another who desires liberation;
but rare indeed is the man of great wisdom who is free from longing for both enjoyment and liberation.
Regarding dharma, wealth, pleasure, and liberation, as well as life and death,
for one of noble mind, there is indeed nothing to be rejected and nothing to be accepted.
He has no desire for the destruction of the world, nor does he have hatred for its continued existence; therefore, like one who lives by his livelihood, he dwells happily and is blessed.

Thinking, "I have achieved my purpose through this knowledge," the successful person, with his conceptual mind dissolved, remains at ease while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, and eating. (Avg 17.8)
View is empty, effort is in vain, and the sense faculties are impaired;
there is neither longing nor detachment for one whose ocean of saṃsāra has been exhausted.
He neither wakes nor sleeps, neither opens nor closes his eyes; oh, the liberated one’s state of mind abides somewhere beyond all else! (Avg 17.10)
Established in his own nature, he is seen everywhere; with a pure intention in all things, liberated from all latent impressions, he shines as one liberated everywhere. (Avg 17.11)
Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, grasping, speaking, and walking—freed from both desired and undesired activities, the person of great vision is truly liberated. (Avg 17.12)
He neither censures nor praises; he neither rejoices nor is angered;
he neither gives nor takes; liberated and dispassionate toward everything. (Avg 17.13)
Upon seeing a woman full of passion, or even death itself approaching, the high-minded man whose mind is unperturbed and who remains composed is truly liberated. (Avg 17.14)
Whether in pleasure or pain, whether regarding a man or a woman, in prosperity or in adversity,
there is no difference at all in the wise person who perceives with equanimity everywhere.
In a person who has exhausted the cycle of existence, there is neither violence nor compassion, neither restlessness nor dejection, neither wonder nor agitation. (Avg 17.16)
Neither a hater of sense objects nor one greedy for them, with a mind always unattached, he experiences both what is obtained and what is not obtained. (Avg 17.17)

One whose mind is empty does not perceive states of concentration or non-concentration, benefit or harm, nor conceptual constructions; he remains as if established in absolute isolation (*kaivalya*). (Avg_17.18)
Free from possessiveness and free from egoism, certain that "nothing exists," with all desires dissolved within, he does not act even while acting.
Free from mental illumination, delusion, sleep,
and lethargy, having reached a certain state, one becomes one whose mind has dissolved.
Aṣṭāvakra said: Homage to that peaceful radiance, whose sole nature is bliss, for whom delusion becomes like a dream upon the dawning of awakening. *Aṣṭāvakra-gītā* 18.1.
Having acquired all forms of wealth, one obtains abundant enjoyments;
yet indeed, without the renunciation of everything, one cannot become happy. (Avg 18.2)
For one whose inner self is consumed by the flames of the sun of suffering that must be endured, whence can there be happiness, except for the downpour of the nectar-stream of tranquility? (Avg 18.3)
This existence is merely a mental construction; in the ultimate sense, it is nothing at all.
For those who discern both existence and non-existence, there is no such thing as non-existence regarding their own mental constructions.
Neither distant nor contracted, the state of the Self is indeed attained—
free from conceptual construction, effortless, changeless, and stainless.
Upon the mere cessation of delusion, by virtue of the simple recovery of their true nature,
those whose vision is unobstructed shine forth, free from sorrow.
"Everything is merely conceptual construction; the self is eternally liberated. Having realized this, why would a wise person practice like a child? (Avg 18.7)
Having realized with certainty that "the Self is Brahman," and that existence and non-existence are merely conceptual constructs,
what does one free from desire perceive, what does he speak, and what does he do?
"‘This is I,’ ‘this is not I’— such conceptual constructions have ceased for the yogin who has become silent, having resolved that all is the Self."
For the yogin who has attained peace, there is neither distraction nor one-pointedness, neither excessive wakefulness nor dullness, neither pleasure nor pain. (Avg 18.10)
Whether in sovereign power or in the life of a mendicant, whether there is gain or loss, whether among people or in the forest,
there is no distinction for the yogi whose nature is free from conceptual construction.
Where is dharma, and where is desire? Where is worldly gain, and where is discernment?
For the yogin who is liberated from the pairs of opposites, there is neither "this has been done" nor "this has not been done."
There is no duty whatsoever to be performed, nor any attachment in the heart;
for the yogi liberated while living, life here is simply as it happens.
Where is delusion, and where is the universe? Where is that meditation, and where is liberation—for the Great Being who has come to rest within the limit of all conceptual constructions?
Let one who claims that this entire universe does not exist indeed be without latent tendencies; for though seeing, he sees nothing at all.
He by whom the Supreme Brahman has been seen should contemplate, "I am that Brahman.
What does he contemplate? He who is free from thought and perceives no second.
He who has perceived the distraction of the self brings about its cessation;
but what can the noble one do, since he is not distracted and there is no [self] to be accomplished? (Avg 18.17)
The steadfast one, though living in a world that is perverted, remains like the world;
yet he perceives neither meditative absorption nor distraction, nor any defilement of his own.
The wise one who is free from existence and non-existence, satisfied and devoid of latent tendencies— nothing at all has been done by him, even though he may act according to worldly perception.
Whether in the midst of worldly activity or in the state of cessation, no difficulty is found by the wise man;
for when whatever must be done comes upon him, he remains at ease after having performed it.
Free from latent tendencies, without support, acting according to its own will, and released from bonds, it moves like a dry leaf when tossed by the wind of formative forces. (Avg 18.21)
But for one who is beyond saṃsāra, there is neither joy nor dejection anywhere;
with a mind eternally cooled, he shines like one who is bodiless. (Avg 18.22)
For the steadfast one who delights in the Self, whose soul is cool and exceedingly clear, there is no desire for anything anywhere, nor is there destruction of anything at all. (Avadānaśataka 18.23)
For this wise one whose mind is by nature empty, even as he acts spontaneously like an ordinary person, there is neither pride nor humiliation. (Avg 18.24)
"This action was performed by the body, not by me whose nature is pure"—he who acts while following such a thought does not truly act. (Avg 18.25)
One who does not speak of that [worldly existence] as if he were still involved in it is no longer a fool;
liberated while living, happy and glorious, he shines even while wandering through saṃsāra. (Avg 18.26)
Exhausted by various discursive thoughts, the steadfast one has attained rest;
he does not conceptualize, he does not know, he does not hear, and he does not see.
Neither the seeker of liberation nor the other [the non-seeker] is liberated through non-concentration and non-distraction;
rather, having ascertained and beholding the imagined, the one of great resolve abides in Brahman alone. (Avg 18.28)
He who possesses internal egoism acts even when he does not act;
by one whose mind is firm and free from egoism, nothing that was uncreated has been created.
Neither agitated nor satisfied, free from agency and devoid of vibration, the mind of the liberated one shines—hopeless and with all doubt gone. (Avg 18.30)
When the mind does not proceed toward either meditative absorption or purposeful activity, it nevertheless meditates and acts, though this is signless (nirnimitta). (Avg 18.31)
Having heard the reality as it truly is, the dull-witted person falls into delusion;
or else, though not deluded, he becomes as if one who is deluded, shrinking back in fear. (Avadānakalpalatā 18.32)
The foolish practice one-pointedness or cessation with great intensity;
the wise, established in their own state, do not perceive any task to be done, remaining as if asleep.
Whether through lack of effort or through effort, the fool does not attain peace;
by the mere certainty of reality, the wise person becomes peaceful. (Avg 18.34)
People devoted to practice do not recognize that Self, which is pure, awakened, dear, full, free from conceptual proliferation, and beyond affliction. Avg_18.35 //
The deluded one does not attain liberation through action, which takes the form of habitual practice;
blessed is he who, through mere higher knowledge, remains liberated and changeless. (Avg 18.36)
The deluded person does not attain that Brahman for which he desires to become; yet the wise one, even without desiring it, partakes in the very nature of the Supreme Brahman. (Avg 18.37)
Those who grasp at objects of perception are without support, deluded, and nourishers of saṃsāra;
the wise have cut the root of this very root of misfortune. (Avg 18.38)
The fool does not find peace, even though he desires to be at peace;
whereas the wise person, having ascertained reality, always possesses a tranquil mind.
Wherein is the vision of that self which relies upon what is seen?
The wise do not see this or that; they see the imperishable self.
Where indeed is cessation for the deluded one who persists in exertion? For the wise man who delights in himself alone, it is always natural.
There is no one who brings an entity into being, nor another who does not bring anything into being; there is someone who brings neither into being—in this very way, one is undisturbed.
Those of inferior intellect meditate on a self that is pure and non-dual;
yet, due to delusion, they do not realize it, remaining unliberated for as long as they live. (Avg 18.43)
For one who desires liberation, the intellect does not exist without an object of support;
however, for the liberated one, the intellect is always free from desire and indeed without any support.
Seeing the island of sense-objects and becoming terrified, those seeking refuge enter its embrace instantly for the sake of achieving restraint and one-pointed concentration. (Avg 18.45)
Having seen Hari, who is free from all latent impressions, the elephants of the sense-objects flee in silence; they are no longer capable of serving him, even though they offer their flatteries.
Free from doubt and with a disciplined mind, he does not cling to the notion of liberation;
seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, and eating, he remains as he is, in comfort. (AvG 18.47)
Merely by hearing the reality, one whose intellect is purified and undisturbed perceives neither right conduct nor misconduct, nor even indifference.
When it is time to do something, the upright person does it—whether it be good or bad—for their activity is indeed like that of a child. (Avg 18.49)
Through sovereignty one attains happiness; through sovereignty one obtains the supreme; through sovereignty one may reach bliss; through sovereignty one reaches the highest state. Avg_18.50 //
When one realizes that one's own self is neither an agent nor an enjoyer, then all fluctuations of the mind are indeed brought to an end. (Avg 18.51)
Even an unrestrained and unartificial state of being shines for the steadfast man;
however, the artificial peace of a fool whose mind is full of longing does not. (Avg 18.52)
Those wise ones, free from conceptual construction, unbound and possessed of liberated intellects, sport with great enjoyments or enter mountain caves. (Avg 18.53)
Upon seeing a learned Vedic scholar, a deity, a sacred ford, a woman, a king, or a beloved, the wise man honors them, yet no latent impression (vāsanā) whatsoever remains in his heart. (Avg 18.54)
Even when laughed at and reviled by servants, sons, wives, grandsons, and kinsmen, the yogi does not undergo even the slightest change of mind. (Avg 18.55)
Though satisfied, he is not satisfied; though weary, he does not grow weary.
Only those like him can understand his various wondrous states. (Avadāna-kalpalatā 18.56)
The very sense of "duty to act" is saṃsāra; the wise do not perceive it, for they are empty in form, formless, changeless, and free from affliction.
One of deluded intellect is distracted everywhere by agitation even when not acting;
whereas one who is skillful remains unperturbed even while performing his duties. (Avg 18.58)
He dwells in happiness, sleeps in happiness, and comes and goes in happiness; he speaks with ease and enjoys his food with ease, his mind remaining tranquil even amidst worldly affairs. (Avg 18.59)
He whose nature is free from affliction, unlike the worldly practitioner, shines beautifully, his defilements gone and as unshakeable as a great lake. (Avg 18.60)
Even for the deluded, cessation results in engagement;
even for the wise, engagement bears the fruit of cessation.
Detachment from possessions is generally seen in the fool;
but for one whose desire for the body has dissolved, where is passion and where is detachment? (Avg 18.62)
The view of the deluded person is always attached to the cultivation of cultivation;
but for one who is established in their own nature, that [view] takes the form of non-view through the cultivation of what is to be cultivated.
The sage who acts like a child, free from desire in all undertakings,
incurs no defilement, even while performing action, for he is pure.
He alone is blessed and a knower of the self who is equanimous toward all states of being—seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, and eating, yet with a mind free from craving. (Avg 18.65)
Where is saṃsāra, and where is its appearance? Where is the goal to be attained, and where is the means? For the wise one who is always free from conceptual construction, these are like space.
He triumphs, having renounced all objects of desire, his body being the very form of the full natural flavor;
he for whom there exists an uncontrived and uninterrupted meditative absorption.
What need is there for much speaking here? One who has realized the truth, the noble-minded one, is free from longing for both enjoyment and liberation, and is always dispassionate toward everything.
The duality of the world, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), is a mere manifestation of names; once this is abandoned, what task remains for pure consciousness? (Avg 18.69)
Having reached the certainty that "all this is born of delusion and nothing exists," the pure one, whose manifestation is unperceivable, subsides by his very nature.

For one whose nature is pure radiance and who perceives no state of being an object, where is there ritual injunction, where is detachment, where is renunciation, or even where is tranquility? (Avg 18.71)
For one who vibrates with infinite forms and does not perceive a primal nature, where is bondage and where is liberation? Where is joy and where is despondency? (Avg 18.72)
In this cycle of existence, which extends as far as the intellect, only illusion manifests;
the wise person shines forth when free from possessiveness, free from egoism, and free from desire.

For the sage who perceives himself as having reached the inexhaustible and free from all distress, where is there knowledge, or where is the universe, or where is the body, or the notions of "I" and "mine"? (Avg 18.74)
If one of dull intellect abandons actions such as cessation,
they immediately fall into the state of pursuing mere mental fantasies and idle chatter.
Even having heard that reality, the dull-witted person does not abandon his delusion;
though free from conceptual construction, through external effort he remains craving for internal objects. (Avg 18.76)
One whose karma has dissolved through wisdom may perform actions even in the sight of the world,
yet finds no opportunity to act or to say anything at all.
Where is darkness, or where is light, and where is there anything to be abandoned—for the wise one who is forever changeless and free from fear? (Avataṃsaka 18.78)
Where is there fortitude, where discernment, or even where fearlessness for the yogin who is of an inexpressible nature and yet devoid of intrinsic nature? (Avg 18.79)
There is neither heaven nor indeed hell, nor even liberation while living;
for what is the use of saying much more here? From the perspective of Yoga, there is nothing at all.
He does not crave gain, nor does he grieve over lack of gain;
the mind of the steadfast one is cool, as if filled with the nectar of immortality.
Free from desire, he praises neither the peaceful nor does he blame the wicked;
equal in suffering and happiness, contented, he perceives no task whatsoever as needing to be done. (Avg 18.82)
The steadfast one does not hate cyclic existence, nor does he seek to behold a self;
liberated from both joy and resentment, he neither dies nor lives.
Free from affection for wife and children, free from desire for sense objects, free from anxiety even regarding his own body, and free from hope—the wise man shines. (Avg 18.84)
The wise man finds contentment everywhere as he follows his natural course,
wandering freely through various lands and sleeping wherever the sun sets.
Whether the body falls or rises, the Great-Souled One has no concern for it,
having forgotten all of saṃsāra through resting in the ground of his own true nature.
Possessing nothing, moving at will, free from the pairs of opposites, with doubts severed,
unattached to all states of being, the wise one rejoices in solitude.
Free from the sense of "mine," the steadfast one shines, for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are equal;
his knots of the heart are thoroughly severed, and passion and ignorance have been shaken off.
For one who is everywhere undistracted, no latent impression remains in the heart;
with whom can a comparison be made for the liberated soul who is free from craving?
Though knowing, he does not know; though seeing, he does not see;
though speaking, he does not speak—who else but one free from latent tendencies could be so? (Avigraha 18.90)
Whether he be a monk or even a king, he who is free from desire shines;
he whose mind has dissolved all notions of beauty and ugliness regarding worldly phenomena.
Where is there freedom of will, where is there constraint, or where is the determination of reality for the yogi who has accomplished his purpose and whose nature is sincere and upright? (Avg 18.92)
How and to whom can that which is experienced within by one who is satisfied in the repose of the self, free from desire, and devoid of suffering, be described?
Though asleep, he does not sleep in deep slumber; though lying down, he is not in a dream;
and even while awake, he does not merely wake—the steadfast one, satisfied at every step.
Though possessing knowledge, he is free from thought; though possessing senses, he is without senses;
though possessing intellect, he is without intellect; though possessing ego, he is without egoism.
Neither happy nor suffering, neither dispassionate nor attached;
neither desiring liberation nor liberated, he is nothing at all, yet not nothing.
Though distracted, he is not distracted; though in meditative absorption, he does not possess [the pride of] absorption.
Though dull, he is not dull; blessed indeed, though wise, he is not a mere scholar. (Avg 18.97)
Liberated, established in his natural state, content because he has fulfilled what was to be done,
and equanimous everywhere due to freedom from craving, he does not dwell upon what was left undone or what was accomplished.
He is not delighted when praised, nor does he become angry when reviled;
he is not agitated by death, nor does he rejoice in life.
One whose mind is tranquil does not run toward a crowd of people, nor toward the forest;
rather, in whatever way and wherever they may be, they remain equanimous.
Janaka said:
Having taken up the forceps of the knowledge of reality from the interior of my heart,
I have extracted the thorns of various kinds of misconceptions.
Where is dharma, and where is desire? Where is wealth, and where is discernment? Where is duality, and where is non-duality, for me who am established in my own greatness?
Where is the past, where is the future, or where even the present?
Where is space, and where is eternity for me, who am established in my own majesty?
Where is the self and where is the non-self? Where is the auspicious and where is the inauspicious?
Where is thought and where is the absence of thought for me, who am established in my own greatness?
Where is dream, or where is deep sleep, and likewise where is waking? And where is the fourth state, or even fear, for me who am established in my own greatness? (Avigita 19.5)
Where is far and where is near? Where is the exterior and where is the interior?
Where is the gross and where is the subtle for me, who am established in my own greatness?

Where is death or life? Where are the worlds? Where is this world, or what belongs to it? Where is dissolution, or where is meditative absorption for me, who am established in my own greatness? (Avg 19.7)
Enough with talk of the three aims of life; enough also with talk of yoga;
enough with talk of specialized knowledge—for me, who have found rest in the Self.
Janaka said:
Where are the elements, where is the body, where are the senses, or where is the mind?
Where is the void and where is desirelessness within my own stainless nature?
Where is the scripture, where is self-knowledge, or where is the mind free from objects?
Where is satisfaction, and where is the state of desirelessness for me, who have forever transcended dualities?
Where is knowledge, and where is ignorance? Where am I, and where is this "mine"?
Where is bondage, and where is liberation? Where is the manifestation of the true nature?
Where are the fruits of past actions (*prārabdha-karma*), and where is liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*)?
And where is that absolute isolation after death (*videhakaivalya*) for one who is eternally without distinction? (Avg 20.4)
Where is the agent, and where is the enjoyer? Where is vibration, which is devoid of action?
Where is the immediate fruit, or where am I, who am eternally without intrinsic nature?
Where is the world, or where is the seeker of liberation? Where is the yogi, or where is the possessor of knowledge? Where is the bound, and where is the liberated? I am my own non-dual nature.
Where is creation and where is dissolution? Where is the goal and where is the means? Where is the practitioner or where is the accomplishment? I am my own non-dual nature.
Where is the knower or the means of knowledge, where is the object of knowledge or the act of knowing?
Where is anything at all, or where is nothing at all, for me who am ever pure? (Avg 20.8)
Where is distraction, and where is one-pointedness? Where is lack of understanding, and where is delusion?
Where is joy, or where is despair, for me who am forever inactive? (Avg 20.9)
Where is this worldly convention, and where is that ultimate reality?
Where is pleasure, and where is pain, for me who am forever devoid of discernment?
Where is illusion and where is cyclic existence? Where is attachment and where is detachment? Where is the individual soul and where is that Brahman—for me, who am eternally pure? (Avg 20.11)
Where is there activity or cessation? Where is liberation or bondage for me, who am eternally established in myself, immutable and undivided? (Avg 20.12)
Where is instruction, or where is scripture; where is the disciple, or where is the teacher;
and where is the human goal for me, who am Śiva, free from all limiting adjuncts?
Where does it exist, and where does it not exist? Where is there one, and where is there two?
What is the use of saying much here? To me, nothing at all arises.
